# Objects and constructors

Tuples are fine for small data unpacked quickly. Once there are ten named fields, repeated
boilerplate, and rules of their own, a tuple starts to hurt. An object gives a name to a set of
fields, and Nim adds a literal constructor that makes it pleasant to use.

This chapter also unpacks one difference that keeps surprising people: value objects and
`ref object`s behave differently when copied. Ignoring that is a classic source of bugs.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can define an `object` and fill it with a constructor, use default values,
tell a value object from a `ref object`, override `$`, and read the `undeclared field` error.
:::

## Defining an object and filling it

Declare the object with `type`, then list the fields below it.

```{.nim}
type Person = object
  name: string
  age: int

let ada = Person(name: "Ada", age: 36)
echo ada.name, " is ", ada.age
```

```{.txt}
Ada is 36
```

`Person(name: "Ada", age: 36)` is the literal constructor. Nim generates it for every object type,
so there is no function to write yourself. A field you leave out takes its default value.

## Fields that may change

Fields may change as long as the variable was declared `var`.

```{.nim}
type Point = object
  x, y: int

var p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
p.x = 10
echo p.x, ",", p.y
```

```{.txt}
10,2
```

`x, y: int` is shorthand for two fields of the same type.

## Object default values

An object declared without a value is safe to use right away; every field holds its type's default.

```{.nim}
type Counter = object
  hits: int
  label: string

var c: Counter
echo c.hits, "|", repr(c.label)
```

```{.txt}
0|""
```

This matches `var` without a value on a primitive type: no garbage memory to worry about.

## Objects already have a `$`

Readers often assume `echo` rejects objects. For value objects, Nim provides a built-in `$`.

```{.nim}
type Person = object
  name: string

echo Person(name: "Ada")
```

```{.txt}
(name: "Ada")
```

The output is the literal form again: field names with their values. Good for a quick inspection,
though usually not pleasant to read.

## Overriding `$` yourself

To change how an object prints, define `$` for that type.

```{.nim}
type Person = object
  name: string
  age: int

proc `$`(p: Person): string =
  p.name & " (" & $p.age & ")"

echo Person(name: "Ada", age: 36)
```

```{.txt}
Ada (36)
```

Once `$` exists, `echo` picks it up automatically. The same rule applies to `&`, string
interpolation, and explicit `$` calls. This is the idiomatic way to give a type a text
representation.

## `ref object`: stored on the heap

A `ref object` keeps its data on the heap, and the variable holds a pointer to it.

```{.nim}
type Node = ref object
  value: int
  next: Node

var head = Node(value: 1)
head.next = Node(value: 2)
echo head.value, " -> ", head.next.value
```

```{.txt}
1 -> 2
```

The `next` field is typed `Node`, a reference to another node. Chained structures like this are
what make `ref` practical. `nil` is a valid value for a reference.

A `ref` declared without a value holds `nil`. To fill it, use `new`.

```{.nim}
type Person = ref object
  name: string

var p = Person(name: "Ada")
echo p.name

var q: Person
new(q)
q.name = "Grace"
echo q.name
```

```{.txt}
Ada
Grace
```

`new(q)` allocates the object and stores it in `q`. A literal constructor such as
`Person(name: "Ada")` does the same thing, then fills the fields.

## The built-in `$` does not cover `ref`

A value object has a built-in `$`, its reference does not.

```{.nim}
type Person = ref object
  name: string

var p = Person(name: "Ada")
echo p
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(5, 1) Error: type mismatch
Expression: echo p
  [1] p: Person

Expected one of (first mismatch at [position]):
[1] proc echo(x: varargs[typed, `$`])
```

The message never says `$` outright, but the last line hints at it: `echo` needs a type that has
one. There are two fixes. First, define `$` for `Person`. Second, dereference with `echo p[]` so the
object's built-in `$` is used.

## Value vs reference: copying is not always the same

The priciest difference between the two shows up when a value is copied.

```{.nim}
type
  Card = object
    points: int
  CardRef = ref object
    points: int

var a = Card(points: 1)
var b = a
b.points = 99
echo "value: ", a.points, " ", b.points

var c = CardRef(points: 1)
var d = c
d.points = 99
echo "ref:   ", c.points, " ", d.points
```

```{.txt}
value: 1 99
ref:   99 99
```

With a value object, `var b = a` copies the whole contents, so changing `b` never touches `a`. With
a `ref object`, `var d = c` copies the pointer, not the data. Both point at the same object, so
changing `d` changes `c` too.

The rule: use `object` for small values you want copied, and `ref object` for large data or when
several parts of the code really must share one value.

## Reading the error: a field that does not exist

Reaching for an undeclared field is rejected by the compiler.

```{.nim}
type Person = object
  name: string

let ada = Person(name: "Ada")
echo ada.email
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(5, 9) Error: undeclared field: 'email'
```

The message names the field it was looking for. Start from the type declaration: `Person` has only
`name`, so `email` truly does not exist. This is the easiest error class to fix, because the answer
lives in the type definition, not in the line that used it. The real message appends
`for type Person`; it is trimmed here.

## Basic inheritance

An object can inherit fields from another object with `object of`.

```{.nim}
type
  Animal = ref object of RootObj
    name: string
  Dog = ref object of Animal
    tricks: int

proc describe(a: Animal): string =
  a.name

var rex = Dog(name: "Rex", tricks: 3)
echo describe(rex), " knows ", rex.tricks, " tricks"
```

```{.txt}
Rex knows 3 tricks
```

`Dog` inherits the `name` field from `Animal` and adds `tricks`. A procedure taking `Animal` also
accepts a `Dog`, because a `Dog` is a more specific `Animal`. Inheritance uses `ref object` with
`RootObj` at the root of the hierarchy.

## Choosing a procedure at runtime

A `proc` picks its version from the static type, not from the object's type at runtime. For behavior
that really depends on the runtime type, Nim has `method`.

```{.nim}
type
  Animal = ref object of RootObj
    name: string
  Dog = ref object of Animal
    tricks: int
  Cat = ref object of Animal

method speak(a: Animal): string {.base.} = a.name & " makes a sound"
method speak(d: Dog): string = d.name & " barks"
method speak(c: Cat): string = c.name & " meows"

let animals: seq[Animal] = @[Dog(name: "Rex", tricks: 3), Cat(name: "Milo")]
for a in animals:
  echo speak(a)
```

```{.txt}
Rex barks
Milo meows
```

Even though `animals` is a `seq[Animal]`, `speak(a)` calls the method of the object's actual type. One
method is marked `{.base.}` as the root of the hierarchy; without that marker the compiler warns
because the old form is deprecated.

For comparison, a `proc` with the same name never looks at the runtime type:

```{.nim}
type
  Animal = ref object of RootObj
    name: string
  Dog = ref object of Animal
  Cat = ref object of Animal

proc speak(a: Animal): string = "a sound"
proc speak(d: Dog): string = "a bark"
proc speak(c: Cat): string = "a meow"

let animals: seq[Animal] = @[Dog(name: "Rex"), Cat(name: "Milo")]
for a in animals:
  echo speak(a)
```

```{.txt}
a sound
a sound
```

Both objects are a `Dog` and a `Cat`, yet the proc that runs is always the `Animal` version. Reach for
`method` only when behavior differs per type; otherwise a `proc` is cheaper and easier to read.

## Exercises

## Exercises

1. Add an `email: string` field to `Person`, fill it with the constructor, then print it.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   type Task = object
     title: string
     done: bool

   var t = Task(title: "write")
   echo t.done, " ", t.title
   ```
3. Write `type Book = ref object of RootObj` with `title` and `pages` fields, create one instance,
   then print it through a procedure that takes a `Book`.
4. The code below fails. Fix it without changing the `let`:
   ```{.nim}
   type Point = object
     x: int

   let p = Point(x: 1)
   p.x = 2
   echo p.x
   ```

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- An `object` groups named fields; `Type(field: value)` is the literal constructor.
- Omitted fields take their type's default, and an object without a value is safe to use.
- Value objects have a built-in `$`; `ref object`s do not, so define `$` or use `p[]`.
- Copying a value object duplicates the data; copying a `ref object` duplicates the pointer.
- `object of RootObj` inherits fields; `new` allocates a `ref` that still holds `nil`.
